takeaway: An antibody-drug conjugate is an antibody, usually IgG, joined by a linker to a cytotoxic payload. Brentuximab vedotin (2011) and T-DM1 (2013) opened the class; nine ADCs were approved by the time of this review [1].
clinicalQuestion: What is an antibody-drug conjugate and which approvals defined the class?
background: The idea is old, but clinical ADCs arrived when linker and payload chemistry became reliable enough for approval [1].
population: Patients treated with approved anticancer ADCs.
primaryOutcome: Structure of the class and the approvals that proved it.
mainFindings: Nine different ADCs had been approved for cancer by publication, with dozens more in development. Brentuximab vedotin, targeting CD30, was approved in 2011 for relapsed/refractory classical Hodgkin lymphoma and systemic ALCL. Ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1), targeting HER2, was approved in 2013 for trastuzumab-resistant metastatic breast cancer. IgG is the predominant antibody backbone. Human IgG has four subclasses that differ in half-life and Fc-receptor binding; IgG3 has generally been avoided because of a relatively short half-life. Cleavable linkers show varying stability and can degrade in plasma [1].
clinicalMeaning: Choose an ADC for its target, not as ordinary chemotherapy. Linker instability in plasma is a real design limit [1].
limitations: The approval count is the count at this 2021 review, not a 2026 formulary [1].
bottomLine: Teach the three-part structure and the two landmark approvals, and do not freeze the class at nine drugs [1].
practiceImplication: Name the antigen (CD30 or HER2) when you name the drug [1].
safetyOutcomes: Plasma degradation of cleavable linkers is a stated limitation.
trustRationale: Expert review in a major oncology journal; approval counts age.
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not say only nine ADCs exist in 2026.
A paper limited to resistance in breast cancer is not the class overview.
